Title: Nobody's Witness
Credit: Written by
Author: [Your Name]
Draft date: September 2026

===

>THE LOOK<

Tokyo as a memory that is still happening.

The city in this film belongs to no single year. Pay phones beside smartphones. Boxy CRT televisions glowing in shop windows. Showa-era vending machines humming on empty corners beneath new glass towers. None of it is ever commented on. It is simply how the world is.

LIGHT. The city lights the characters, not the sky: vending machines, shop signs, train windows, fluorescent tubes. Sodium orange against a sick fluorescent green. Soft halation around every light, blacks slightly crushed. It should look like film, and feel like something remembered.

RAIN. Never glamorous. No lightning, no storms. Cold, steady, patient rain that turns the streets black and reflective.

CAMERA. Wide and patient. Close-ups are rare, so they count. We watch people inside the city, not apart from it.

SOUND. Real Tokyo sounds, placed slightly wrong: a crossing melody for an empty street, a television laughing in an empty room. Music arrives late, and sparingly.

OTHER LIVES. There is always a sign of other people -- a lit window, a radio through a wall, laundry overhead. Every private moment happens among thousands of others.

!NOTHING IS EXPLAINED.

LANGUAGE. The Voss sisters speak English to each other. Dialogue marked (in Japanese) is spoken in Japanese and subtitled in English.

REFERENCE POINTS. Ozu's TOKYO STORY for restraint. KOWLOON GENERIC ROMANCE and the 1997 illustrated Kowloon Walled City panoramas for density, texture and memory.

===

FADE IN:

EXT. BACKSTREET, KANDA - NIGHT

Rain. Not a storm. Just cold, steady, patient rain.

A narrow street of shuttered shops. A vending machine hums on the corner. High up, one lit window, a radio playing behind it.

MARA VOSS (24) stands in the dark doorway of a closed barber's, soaked, no umbrella. Her phone lights up: VERA. She watches it ring.

MARA
(to the phone)
Not tonight.

She declines it.

An OLD MAN (70s) comes slowly up the street in a good coat gone thin at the cuffs. He sees her in the doorway and stops. Something in his face gives way.

OLD MAN
(in Japanese; to himself)
Twenty years.

Behind him, a MASKED MAN steps out of the dark and makes a small, correct bow.

MASKED MAN
(in Japanese; quietly; subtitled: "Excuse me.")
Shitsurei shimasu.

Two shots, flat and small in the rain. The old man folds onto the street.

The masked man touches his ear.

MASKED MAN
(in Japanese)
First position done. Moving to second.

He walks back the way he came, to a dark car idling at the far end of the street. He doesn't hurry. He never looks at the doorway.

Mara runs to the old man. Her bag slides off her shoulder and spills across the wet street. She doesn't notice.

MARA
(whispering)
Mr. Sakai?

MARA
It's okay -- I'll get someone --
(in halting Japanese)
Ambulance. I'll call. Ambulance.

His hand comes out of his coat with something small and brass in it. He presses it into her palm and closes her fingers over it.

OLD MAN
(in Japanese)
Don't let them have it.

MARA
(in halting Japanese)
Have what? I don't --

He's gone. Rain in his open eyes.

In her hand: a small brass key on a stamped number tag.

The dark car pulls away and takes the long way round the block. At the other end of the street, the amber glow of a bar. Mara runs for it.

Behind her, on the street: her purse, open in the rain.

CUT TO:



INT. SMALL BAR, KANDA - CONTINUOUS

Six stools and a counter. Shelves of bottles glowing amber. On a high shelf, an old CRT television plays a late-night variety show, sound low. Rain drums on the roof.

A man in a raincoat on the far stool, a notebook beside a beer gone flat: the JOURNALIST (40s). Nobody behind the counter. Crates clatter somewhere in the back.

Mara bursts in, the key in her fist.

JOURNALIST
Miss Voss?

He knows her name. Before she can answer, the door opens behind her. Rain noise.

MASKED MAN
(in Japanese; quietly; subtitled: "Excuse me.")
Shitsurei shimasu.

The same words. Mara is behind the counter before she knows she's moved.

JOURNALIST
(in Japanese)
Where is he?

Two shots. On the high shelf, the television audience laughs.

Behind the counter, Mara folds herself into the gap between the crates and the ice bin. A hair clip slides out of her wet hair and skitters under the shelf. She doesn't breathe.

MASKED MAN
(in Japanese)
Second position done.

He takes one step toward the counter. A voice in his earpiece: one word. He turns and goes.

The door swings shut. The television laughs again.

>CUT TO BLACK.

Over black: RAIN.

>NOBODY'S WITNESS<

>MAIN TITLES<

EXT. VERA'S APARTMENT BUILDING - DUSK

SUPER: "THREE DAYS LATER"

An old four-story apartment block squeezed between newer buildings. Laundry left out on a balcony, getting rained on. A train slides past on the elevated line behind it, windows lit, and the whole building trembles faintly.

One window on the third floor is lit.

INT. VERA'S APARTMENT - CONTINUOUS

Small and tidy. Grey light through rain-streaked glass. A smartphone on the table; an old boxy television in the corner. Nothing here quite belongs to one decade.

By the door, in the umbrella stand: a pale blue umbrella. Bone dry.

On a shelf, one framed photograph, its colors gone warm and faded. A Tokyo street, twenty years ago. An American man in a rumpled suit, smiling, holding the hands of two small girls: VERA (9), serious, and MARA (4), mid-laugh. Behind them, the sign of a noodle shop.

VERA VOSS (29) sits at the low table. Two cups. Hers holds cold tea. The other is empty and clean, set out as though someone is expected.

Through the thin wall, a neighbour's radio plays an old ballad, muffled: a woman's voice, a slow saxophone, a song from another decade. Vera doesn't seem to hear it.

Her phone lies face up in front of her. She calls. Waits.

MARA (V.O.)
(recorded; bright)
It's Mara. You know what to do.

BEEP.

Vera opens her mouth. For a moment, nothing.

VERA
It's me again.
(beat)
I'm not angry anymore. I wasn't really angry then, either. Whatever that man wants, it doesn't matter. I just --
(stops herself)
You left your umbrella. You'll get soaked.
(beat)
Just call me. You don't have to say anything. Just call, so I know.

She hangs up.

The old television murmurs to itself.

NEWS REPORTER (ON TV)
(in Japanese)
...police in Kanda are investigating a double shooting in a small bar in the early hours of Sunday. Two men were killed. Officers say it appears to be a dispute between criminal groups. No arrests have been made...

WEATHER ANNOUNCER (ON TV)
(in Japanese)
...rain continuing through the rest of the week...

She looks at the umbrella by the door. At the clean, empty cup. At the photograph.

She stands. Puts on her coat. Hesitates at the door.

Then she takes the blue umbrella. Mara's umbrella.

The door closes behind her. Through the wall, the song on the neighbour's radio ends. A DJ murmurs something. Rain.

CUT TO:

INT. POLICE STATION, FRONT COUNTER - NIGHT

Fluorescent tubes, one of them flickering. A long counter. Faded posters about pickpockets and traffic safety. An old fax machine beside a new flat monitor. A wall clock that runs a minute fast.

Vera stands at the counter, the closed blue umbrella dripping onto the linoleum.

A YOUNG OFFICER takes her details with polite boredom. Vera's Japanese is fluent, but careful and slightly formal -- learned as a child, relearned as an adult.

YOUNG OFFICER
(in Japanese)
Your sister's age?

VERA
(in Japanese)
Twenty-four.

YOUNG OFFICER
(in Japanese)
Adults sometimes go away for a few days. Especially foreigners. It's usually --

VERA
(in Japanese)
She doesn't. Not without telling me.

He types the name. ON THE MONITOR: MARA VOSS.

He stops typing.

He looks at the screen a moment too long. Then he picks up the desk phone and turns away from her.

YOUNG OFFICER
(in Japanese; quietly, into phone)
Yes. That name. Yes -- the sister is here now.

He hangs up. His manner has changed. Politer.

YOUNG OFFICER (CONT'D)
(in Japanese)
Someone will be right with you.

Vera looks at him. He doesn't meet her eyes.

INT. POLICE STATION, INTERVIEW ROOM - MOMENTS LATER

Small. A table, two chairs, a box of tissues nobody has touched in years. Rain on a frosted window.

DETECTIVE ISHIDA (50s) sets a paper cup of tea in front of Vera. Gentle. Unhurried. Tired, in a way that looks like decency.

ISHIDA
You must be cold.

His English is excellent.

VERA
(in Japanese)
I speak Japanese.

ISHIDA
Of course. But this is a difficult thing. It is easier in your own language.

A small beat. She lets it go. For now.

VERA
The officer looked at the screen and made a phone call. Then you came. What's on the screen?

ISHIDA
Nothing is wrong. We just like to take care with these things.
(sits)
Voss. You grew up here?

VERA
Until I was nine. What's on the screen?

He smiles, as if she has passed a small test.

ISHIDA
When did you last see your sister?

VERA
Three days ago. At my apartment. We had dinner.

ISHIDA
And how did she seem?

Vera hesitates.

VERA
(too quickly)
Normal.

Ishida waits, kindly, as if he knows there is more. She doesn't give it.

ISHIDA
Did she ever mention Kanda? Friends there? Work?

Vera's eyes go to the frosted window before she answers.

VERA
Kanda? No. Why --

She stops. Something arrives in her face.

VERA (CONT'D)
The shootings. In Kanda. It was on the news.

Ishida says nothing. That is its own answer.

VERA (CONT'D)
Is she hurt?

ISHIDA
We have no reason to believe she is hurt.

VERA
That's not the same as saying she isn't.

ISHIDA
Miss Voss --

VERA
Is she dead?

ISHIDA
We have no reason to believe she is dead.

She hears it: the careful, official shape of the sentence. Her hand tightens around the paper cup.

VERA
Stop saying that. Stop saying what you have no reason to believe and tell me what you know.

ISHIDA
What I know is that two men were killed in Kanda, and that it is a matter between criminal groups. And that your sister is a young woman who has not called her sister for three days.
(beat)
Those may be two separate things.

VERA
May be.

ISHIDA
May be.

The cup crumples in her fist. Hot tea runs over her fingers and onto the table. She doesn't seem to feel it.

For the first time in years, someone takes a tissue from the box. Ishida does, and offers it to her. She doesn't take it. He sets it down beside her hand.

When she speaks again, it's in Japanese. Low. Precise. Every word placed.

VERA (CONT'D)
(in Japanese)
She is my sister. I have been calling her for three days. If you know where she is, tell me.

Ishida looks at her a long moment. And when he answers, it is in Japanese too, for the first time. Formal. Quiet. A door closing.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
I do not know where she is. That is the truth.
(beat)
And if she saw something she should not have, then the safest place for her is wherever she is now. And the safest thing you can do is nothing.

Silence. Rain on the frosted window.

He switches back to English, gentle again, as if the last minute didn't happen.

ISHIDA (CONT'D)
Go home, Miss Voss. Keep your phone on. If she calls, call me first. Any hour.

He slides his card across the wet table. She looks at it. Then takes it. Stands. Picks up the blue umbrella.

At the door:

VERA
You would have told me if she was dead. Wouldn't you?

ISHIDA
Of course.

She looks at him. She can't tell. She goes. The door closes behind her.

Ishida sits alone a moment. He wipes the spilled tea from the table with the tissue, slowly, carefully, until there is no trace of it.

INT. POLICE STATION, DETECTIVES' ROOM - CONTINUOUS

Rows of cluttered desks under humming fluorescent light. Most are empty at this hour. A radio plays low somewhere.

Ishida sits at his desk and opens the bottom drawer. The two drawers above it stay closed.

.INSERT - THE DRAWER

Inside the drawer, sealed together in one clear evidence bag: Mara's purse and the torn strap, coiled beside it. Still damp.

.BACK TO SCENE

He looks at it a long moment. Closes the drawer.

On the wall, the clock runs a minute fast.

CUT TO:

INT. SMALL BAR, KANDA - DAY

The same bar in flat grey daylight. It looks smaller without the night. Chairs up on the counter. The CRT television is dark.

Where the journalist fell, there is a new rubber floor mat, too clean for this room.

OKADA (60s), the bar's owner, mops around it without looking at it. He has the stillness of a man who hasn't slept.

The door opens. Vera, the blue umbrella in her hand.

OKADA
(in Japanese; not looking up)
We're closed.

Vera holds up her phone: a photo of Mara, laughing at a party, a paper crown on her head.

VERA
(in Japanese)
My sister. Four nights ago. Was she here?

Okada looks at the photo for exactly one second.

OKADA
(in Japanese)
No.

VERA
(in Japanese)
You didn't look.

OKADA
(in Japanese)
I looked. No.

His eyes go, just once, to the far end of the counter. Then back to the mop.

Vera sees it. She doesn't push. She bows, small and polite, and leaves.

She has left the blue umbrella leaning against a stool.

Okada looks at the umbrella for a long moment.

EXT. KANDA STREET - CONTINUOUS

Rain. Vera walks away down the narrow street, no umbrella, head down.

OKADA (O.S.)
(in Japanese)
Miss.

She turns. Okada stands in the bar doorway holding the blue umbrella, out of breath, as if deciding something cost him more than the walk.

He hands it to her. Then he holds out his other hand. In it: the small red enamel bird clip.

Vera stops breathing.

VERA
It was mine. She took it when we were kids. She never gave it back.

She has said it in English, without realizing. Okada doesn't understand the words. He understands her face.

OKADA
(in Japanese)
Behind the counter. After.

VERA
(in Japanese)
Did you give this to the police?

OKADA
(in Japanese)
They didn't ask.

He takes a business card from his apron and presses it into her hand. Old, soft at the corners, handwritten on the back.

OKADA (CONT'D)
(in Japanese)
Not the police. Him.

VERA
(in Japanese)
Who is he?

OKADA
(in Japanese)
He found my daughter once. When no one else would look.

He goes back inside before she can thank him.

Vera looks at the card. Printed in English and in katakana: JACK. INVESTIGATIONS. An address. No surname.

INT. JACK'S OFFICE - NIGHT

Second floor of an old building pressed against the elevated railway. One room. Frosted glass door, JACK hand-lettered on it in English and in katakana.

A desk. A black rotary phone. Filing cabinets. A small CRT television on the cabinet, muted, playing an old black-and-white samurai film. A sofa that has clearly been slept on.

A TRAIN passes outside. The blinds shiver. A spoon rattles in an empty cup. Then silence again.

JACK (48) sits at the desk eating a convenience-store rice ball, watching the silent swordsmen. Handsome once, in a way he stopped maintaining. A good coat, badly kept. He flicks an old steel lighter open and shut, open and shut. There are no cigarettes anywhere.

A knock on the frosted glass. Vera comes in, wet, the blue umbrella dripping.

VERA
(in Japanese)
Are you the one they call Jack?

JACK
(in Japanese)
Who calls me that?

VERA
(in Japanese)
Mr. Okada. The bar in Kanda.

Jack puts the rice ball down.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Sit down.

She sits. He doesn't switch to English. He lets her speak in the language she chose. She notices.

VERA
(in Japanese)
My sister has been missing for four days. The police say to go home and wait.

JACK
(in Japanese)
I don't do missing persons. People who go missing usually want to.

She places the red bird clip on his desk.

VERA
(in Japanese)
She was in that bar. The night two men were shot there.

Jack looks at the clip for a long moment. The lighter stops.

JACK
(in Japanese)
What did the police tell you?

VERA
(in Japanese)
To go home.

JACK
(in Japanese)
It's good advice.

VERA
(in Japanese)
Is it yours, too?

He doesn't answer. Another train passes. The blinds shiver.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Do you have photographs of her?

She takes an envelope from her bag. As she pulls out the photos, something slides out with them and falls face up on the desk:

The old framed photograph from her shelf, taken out of its frame. Twenty years ago. The American man in the rumpled suit. The two small girls. The noodle shop sign behind them.

Jack looks at it.

He does not move. On the TV behind him, a sword is drawn in total silence.

VERA
That's us. Before we left.

She has slipped into English. So does he, quietly.

JACK
Your father.

VERA
He died. That year. Here.

Jack picks the photograph up by its edges, carefully, the way you'd handle evidence. Or something fragile. He looks a moment too long at the noodle shop sign. Then he sets it down, face up, and squares it to the edge of the desk.

JACK
I'm sorry.

VERA
It was a long time ago.

JACK
Yes.

A beat.

JACK (CONT'D)
Ten thousand yen a day. Plus expenses. I'll need a key to her apartment, her phone number, her friends, where she worked, where she drank.

VERA
So you'll look.

JACK
I'll look.

She gathers the photographs. Leaves the red bird clip where it is. He doesn't give it back, and she doesn't ask.

At the door, she stops.

VERA
Mr. Okada said you found his daughter.

JACK
I found her.

VERA
Was she alive?

Jack looks at her. The honest answer is in the pause.

JACK
Her Japanese. Your sister's. Is it good?

VERA
Some. Badly.

JACK
Then she stands out. That helps.

Vera nods. Goes. Through the frosted glass, her shape goes down the stairs and is gone.

Jack sits very still.

INT. JACK'S OFFICE - LATER

Past midnight. Only the desk lamp and the grey flicker of the television, now showing static.

Jack crouches at the grey steel cupboard under the window, pulls its door open and takes out a cardboard box he has kept behind the files. Dust on the lid. He hasn't opened it in years.

Inside: a police notebook. An old ID card with a younger face. A folded newspaper clipping.

.INSERT - THE CLIPPING

An English-language newspaper, yellowed. A small headline: AMERICAN INSURANCE INVESTIGATOR FOUND DEAD - POLICE RULE SUICIDE. A photograph: the same man from Vera's picture. The caption: DANIEL VOSS, 41.

.BACK TO SCENE

Beneath the clipping, one more photograph. Two men at a tiny noodle counter, laughing, steam in the air: DANIEL VOSS, and a much younger JACK, still in a cheap police-issue suit.

Behind them, the same noodle shop sign.

Jack looks at it for a long time.

Then he dials the rotary phone. It takes a long time to dial.

ISHIDA (V.O.)
(in Japanese; filtered)
It's late, Jack.

JACK
(in Japanese)
The Voss girl came to see me.

ISHIDA (V.O.)
(in Japanese)
I know.

Silence on the line. Rain on the window.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Her sister was in that bar.

ISHIDA (V.O.)
(in Japanese)
The sister is a missing persons case. The bar is a gang matter. Two separate things.

JACK
(in Japanese)
And the old man in the street?

ISHIDA (V.O.)
(in Japanese)
Sakai.
(beat)
Yes. That Sakai. I know what you're thinking. Old debts, old enemies. It's a gang matter.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Twenty years, Ishida.

A long pause.

ISHIDA (V.O.)
(in Japanese; gently)
Go to sleep, Jack. You found enough twenty years ago. You're too old to be haunted.

The line goes dead.

Jack holds the receiver a moment longer. He sets it down. Flicks the lighter open. Shut.

A train passes. The photograph of the two laughing men trembles on the desk.

EXT. BACKSTREET, KANDA - NIGHT

The street from the cold open. The rain hasn't stopped in four days.

Jack walks it slowly, a cheap clear plastic umbrella over his head. Not searching. Looking.

The vending machine at the corner. He feeds it a coin. A can of hot coffee drops.

VENDING MACHINE
(recorded; in Japanese)
Thank you very much.

He holds the can without drinking it and looks at the spot where Sakai died. Nothing there now. Rain on asphalt.

He turns and looks at the barbershop doorway. Steps into it. Stands exactly where Mara stood.

From here, he can see the whole street. And, at the far end, the small lit sign of Okada's bar.

He looks at the barbershop pole beside him. Crouches.

Caught on a rough metal edge at knee height: a short twist of torn leather strap.

He doesn't touch it. He looks from the strap, to the spot where Sakai fell, to the bar sign. Reconstructing it.

A shutter RATTLES up above him. A BARBER (80s), in pajamas, looks down from the upstairs window.

BARBER
(in Japanese)
Police again?

JACK
(in Japanese)
Not for a long time.

The barber considers him.

BARBER
(in Japanese)
I told them. I was asleep. I heard the shot. Then a car.

JACK
(in Japanese)
One car?

BARBER
(in Japanese)
One car. Twice.
(beat)
It left. Then it came back.

Jack looks down the empty street.

JACK
(quietly, in Japanese)
Why come back?

Jack doesn't answer. He looks down the street at the drains, the doorways, the gutter: everywhere a small thing could fall.

The barber shrugs and pulls the shutter down.

He looks again at the doorway. At the bar sign. At the torn strap.

She was here. She saw it. She ran there. She saw that too.

And whatever they came back for, she has it.

He looks down the empty street at the bar sign. And one more question he can't answer yet: what was an American girl doing in a Kanda backstreet at one in the morning?

Jack drops the unopened coffee into the recycling bin. The can CLANKS. The crossing melody starts up somewhere, for no one.

INT. MARA'S APARTMENT - DAY

A tiny studio in an old building. Grey daylight. Clothes on every surface. Sketches taped to the walls: pencil, charcoal, cheap watercolour. Trains. Rooftops. Laundry lines. Faces on the subway.

The room smells of someone who meant to come back.

Vera stands just inside the door. She hasn't taken her coat off. Jack moves through the room slowly, touching nothing yet. Looking.

JACK
When were you last here?

VERA
A week ago. She made me coffee. It was terrible.

Jack opens the fridge. Milk. A half-eaten cake in a box. He closes it.

JACK
She wasn't planning to disappear.

VERA
No.

He crouches by the futon. A suitcase underneath, packed and zipped. He looks at it, then at Vera.

VERA (CONT'D)
That was for America. She'd booked a flight. Next month.

JACK
You didn't want her to go.

VERA
I didn't want her to run away again.
(beat)
That's what I said. The night she left. That she always runs.

She looks at the wall of drawings, not at him.

VERA (CONT'D)
It was about Dad. It's always about Dad. She wanted to dig it all up. Who he was here. Why he --
(beat)
I told her to leave him dead.
(beat)
She said I was the one who ran. All the way back here, chasing a ghost, and I won't even look at it.
(beat)
I told her to go, then. Go home. Those were the last things I said to her.

Jack says nothing. He knows better than to comfort it away.

On the desk: a thick sketchbook, its cover soft with use. Jack opens it.

Page after page of the same place. A tiny noodle counter under a railway. Six stools. A curtain. A hand-painted sign. Drawn over and over, from different angles, in different years of her hand -- a child's crayon version taped inside the cover, the newest in careful ink.

JACK
She drew this a lot.

Vera glances over.

VERA
Since she was little. It's from a story I used to tell her. About the noodle shop Dad took us to. She was too young to remember it, so I told her.
(small smile)
She made it up from what I said. It's not real.

Jack turns a page. The sign, in careful ink. Every stroke of the kanji correct.

He has seen this sign. Twice this week. Once in a photograph on Vera's shelf. Once in a box in his own cupboard.

JACK
Can I borrow this?

VERA
Why?

Jack doesn't answer. He looks at the drawing a moment too long.

Vera takes the hair clip out of her coat pocket and sets it on the sketchbook.

VERA
Take this too. It's mine. She stole it.

He takes both.

She hesitates, then nods. He closes the sketchbook and puts it under his arm, and says nothing else about it.

EXT. THE HIVE - DAY

Rain. A wide street of new glass towers and chain stores.

Between two towers, a long white construction hoarding: KUROSE DEVELOPMENT, and a painted plaza full of smiling people who don't exist. Behind it, low and dark and patched, the Hive.

A dense, self-built block of stacked homes and workshops rising eleven storeys, balconies bolted onto balconies, air conditioners and pipes and laundry and hand-painted signs, all of it crushed together under the curve of the elevated railway. The city has grown up around it and forgotten it is there.

At the back, the tower steps down to a low rear wing pressed hard against the concrete railway viaduct, its roof level with the tracks. Old neon signs hang dead on its face. Even in daylight the Hive sits in its own haze of steam and kitchen smoke, as if it had its own weather.

Jack stands on the pavement with the sketchbook under his coat. He looks up at the Hive for a long moment, as if at someone he used to know.

Then he goes in.

INT. THE HIVE, PASSAGES - CONTINUOUS

Narrow corridors, barely shoulder-wide, lit by bare bulbs. Water drips from somewhere above and runs along the floor in a thin shining line. Pipes overhead. Wires everywhere. What daylight gets in comes in thin cold shafts from gaps far overhead, thick with drifting steam.

Doors stand open onto other lives. A MAN at a bench mending radios, a dozen of them murmuring different stations at once. A FAMILY eating dinner at four in the afternoon, the TV loud. An OLD WOMAN asleep in front of a sumo match. A dentist's chair behind a curtain, a hand-lettered price list taped to the wall.

Jack walks through it all. Nobody stops him. Everybody sees him.

A TRAIN passes overhead. The whole building trembles. Dust sifts down through the bulb light. Nobody looks up.

He turns a corner and stops.

The noodle counter. Six stools. The curtain. The hand-painted sign, faded almost to nothing but unmistakable.

It is exactly the drawing.

INT. KANEKO'S NOODLE COUNTER - CONTINUOUS

Steam. A single fluorescent tube. Two customers slurping in silence at the far end.

Behind the counter, KANEKO (70s), tiny and sharp-eyed, works a pot with long chopsticks. She looks up as Jack sits on the fourth stool, beside the third.

She looks at him for a long time. Longer than a stranger would.

KANEKO
(in Japanese)
You got old.

JACK
(in Japanese)
So did you.

KANEKO
(in Japanese)
I was already old. You were a boy in a cheap suit, the only foreign face on the force. Japanese papers, American face. You came here with the American.
(beat)
You always sat there. He sat there.
(beat)
Everything is going. We are just slower.

She looks at the empty third stool beside him.

Jack looks at the third stool, empty beside him, and then at the counter under his hands.

JACK
(in Japanese)
I'm looking for his daughter. The younger one.

Kaneko's chopsticks don't pause.

KANEKO
(in Japanese)
The little one? She was four years old. She ate rice with her fingers.

JACK
(in Japanese)
She's twenty-four now. And someone wants to kill her.

The two customers at the end of the counter have stopped slurping.

Kaneko sets a bowl of noodles in front of Jack.

KANEKO
(in Japanese)

Sakai.

(in Japanese)

(in Japanese)

JACK
(in Japanese)

(in Japanese)

Eat.

For making me.
